content:
The U.S. Navy has scrapped its reported plan to rename an aircraft carrier meant to honor a Black World War II hero after President Donald Trump.

In August, CNN reported on efforts to possibly change the name of the USS Doris Miller, which recognizes a late sailor who defended the U.S. during Japan’s 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, by switching it to Trump, citing “internal discussions.”

Meghan Stoltzfus, director of communications for the Navy, shut down that speculation over the weekend, telling USA Today in an emailed statement there is “no intention” to change the USS Doris Miller’s name while confirming the carrier’s traditional keel-laying ceremony will take place Dec. 5.

The news was applauded by Miller’s great-nephew, Thomas Bledsoe, who told USA Today, “Doris Miller’s legacy is not just our family’s history; it is American history.”

“His courage deserves to be remembered, honored, and recognized for generations to come,” Bledsoe added, while confirming that he and other family members would be in attendance at the keel-laying ceremony next month.

Exactly how far along discussions of the potential Trump renaming had gone remains unclear. At the time of CNN’s initial report, the Navy had no comment, while a Defense Department spokesperson said they had nothing to announce at the time.

In an interview with NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth in September, Miller’s family said they were disappointed by the report.

“We were all overjoyed for them to be giving him that honor,” Miller’s niece, Sherri Miller, told the outlet at the time. “So it was very disheartening to think that the Navy might go back on their word about that.”

A Texas native, Miller was assigned to the USS West Virginia in 1940. During the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, he was one of the last three men to leave his vessel after it began to sink and helped carry many wounded sailors to safety, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

The following year, Miller was presented with the Navy Cross by Adm. Chester W. Nimitz, becoming the first Black man to receive the honor. He continued to serve in the Navy until Nov. 24, 1943, when his carrier, the USS Liscome Bay, was torpedoed in the Pacific Ocean. Though his body was never recovered, Miller was declared killed in action at 24 years old.

Miller’s image famously appeared on Navy recruitment posters in 1943, and his legacy has lived on in popular culture. In 2001, he was portrayed in the film “Pearl Harbor” by actor Cuba Gooding Jr.

The USS Doris Miller will be the first U.S. aircraft carrier named for a Black American, and the first named in honor of an enlisted sailor. At present, it is expected to enter active service around 2034.
